subtype: Approach: asking a parent to pack it for him [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday night. Akash's mother packed his bag as always, humming while he watched television. Akash never looked at what went in.

Wednesday night. Mummy left for a cousin's wedding in another town. "Pack your own bag, beta," she said on the phone. Akash stared at the timetable and could not tell which day it was for.

Thursday. He reached school with the Hindi reader, the wrong maths book and no drawing file. Tanvir shared his book in maths, but the teacher wrote a remark in the diary, and Akash sat out drawing with an empty page.

qa.q: Why did Akash's mother leave on Wednesday night?
qa.a: She left for a cousin's wedding in another town.

qa.q: What was Akash probably feeling when he stared at the timetable on Wednesday night?
qa.a: He was likely confused and a little anxious, because he never watched what went in and could not tell which day it was for.

qa.q: What other approach could Akash try, and why?
qa.a: Akash could learn to read the timetable and pack with his mother watching a few times, so he is ready when she is away. A list on the wall could also guide him.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Akash's wrong books?
qa.a: Tanvir was willing to share his book, which suggests he sees a boy in trouble and wants to help him get through the lesson.

grounding: A boy who lets his mother pack every night cannot manage when she is away and arrives with the wrong books.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to pack it for him [Pitfall]
passage: Disha, you want Ammi to pack your bag every night? Let your Rehana Dadi tell you about your Abbu, Arif. When he was nine, I packed his bag every single night. He never once looked at the timetable. Then my cousin's wedding came, in Hyderabad, and I was away three days. The first morning, Arif packed alone. He put in Monday's books on a Thursday, because Monday was the only day he remembered. No science book, no English notebook. His teacher sent a note home with 'unprepared again' underlined twice. When I came back, he was waiting at the door, not to hug me, but to ask, 'Ammi, how do I read the timetable?'

qa.q: How long was Rehana away for the wedding?
How might young Arif have felt when the teacher's note came home?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and helpless, having never learned to read the timetable himself.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have prevented Arif's trouble?
qa.a: Arif learning to pack from the timetable himself, with his Ammi checking at first, instead of her doing it every night.

qa.q: How did Arif's teacher see those days?
qa.a: The teacher only saw a boy arriving without the right books and underlined 'unprepared again', not knowing his mother usually packed for him.

grounding: Shows a boy who relied on his mother to pack his bag and, when she was away for a wedding, arrived with the wrong books.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to pack it for him [Pitfall]
passage: Every night Rafiq's mother, Nirmala, packed his school bag while he watched cartoons. This week she had gone to a wedding in Pune, and on Tuesday night the power went out in a thunderstorm. Rafiq sat by a candle with his bag and the timetable, but the page looked like a code: periods, numbers, 'SST', 'EVS'. He'd never read it. He shoved in whatever looked familiar and went to bed. Wednesday at school: a Hindi book on a day with no Hindi, no maths notebook, and the drawing book for a class that was on Friday. Two teachers wrote in his diary. On the phone that evening, he asked his mother, very quietly, to teach him the timetable.

qa.q: What did Rafiq bring that he didn't need on Wednesday?
qa.a: A Hindi book on a day with no Hindi, and the drawing book for a class that was on Friday.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when he asked his mother on the phone?
qa.a: Asking 'very quietly' suggests he felt embarrassed and a little ashamed after two teachers wrote in his diary.

qa.q: What should change after this week?
qa.a: Nirmala could teach him to read the timetable and let him pack while she checks; relying on her left him lost when she was away.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see the phone call?
qa.a: Nirmala might feel sorry that her packing left him lost, and glad that he asked to learn.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who depends on his mother to pack his bag and, with her away at a wedding, takes the wrong books to school.
